content: The HCV core antigen (HCVcAg) test demonstrates high specificity and does not necessitate confirmatory testing. However, its cost-effectiveness is limited to settings with very high prevalence. A significant limitation of the HCVcAg test is its lower clinical sensitivity compared to HCV RNA testing, which may result in missed cases, particularly in individuals with low circulating HCV RNA levels. Consequently, the use of dried blood spot testing for HCVcAg is currently not feasible. To streamline the diagnostic process, it is preferable to select an assay that can be utilized both for diagnosing active infection and for confirming treatment success. Based on the limited evidence available, the HCVcAg assay cannot be recommended as a reliable test of sustained virologic response (SVR) when compared to HCV RNA nucleic acid testing (NAT) assays. A survey on values and preferences for future HCV testing strategies revealed that respondents favored a single-step diagnostic approach using a low-cost point-of-care (POC) test to confirm viremia. Among respondents, 52% preferred HCV RNA NAT due to its high sensitivity, while 35% opted for HCVcAg testing because of its lower cost and ease of use. Over half of the respondents were willing to accept a sensitivity reduction to 95% in exchange for a lower test cost. Additionally, 47% preferred tests using capillary blood, which are more suitable for POC settings, even at the expense of sensitivity. A short turnaround time, ideally same-day results, was also a key consideration to minimize loss to follow-up, reduce transportation costs, and allow providers to see more patients in a day. Overall, 88% of respondents supported the idea of a single-step diagnostic strategy, with 96% of people who currently or formerly injected drugs expressing agreement. The primary reasons cited were the ability to rapidly confirm a diagnosis (81%) and initiate treatment (76%). Furthermore, 93% of respondents expressed a strong preference for conducting both initial screening and confirmatory viral load testing at the same location for convenience (70%) and at community-friendly sites (60%). A 2017 survey of hepatitis testing in 19 lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) found that NAT for HCV RNA was available at only one-third of sites, and 40% of countries surveyed had no access to NAT for HCV diagnosis. The HCVcAg assay was not available at any site. The cost of quantitative NAT varies significantly, ranging from $30 to $200 per test, with laboratory equipment being expensive and requiring specialized training for technicians. The cost of HCVcAg testing is currently $25–50, comparable to qualitative NAT ($43–51), but remains a significant barrier to widespread use. Operational considerations for implementing POC HCV viral load testing in community-based clinics, such as those in Yangon, Myanmar, highlight the importance of site-specific factors. These include the cost and ease of use of POC RNA NAT technologies versus laboratory-based assays, as well as the characteristics of the testing site, such as infrastructure, storage facilities, staff skills, and cost. POC assays may be particularly beneficial for vulnerable populations, such as people who inject drugs or those in prisons, where loss to follow-up is high, or in remote locations. While POC assays can expedite viremia confirmation, centralized laboratory systems have also proven effective when supported by efficient specimen transport and rapid electronic result delivery. Priority settings for POC HCV RNA NAT platforms include locations with high-risk populations, such as harm reduction sites for people who inject drugs or prisons, where rapid diagnosis and treatment initiation can improve treatment completion rates. Innovative strategies, such as mobile units offering same-day testing and treatment initiation, have also shown promise in reaching hard-to-reach populations. Evidence suggests that the best outcomes for POC assays occur when they are used at the point of care rather than in distant laboratories. The WHO now recommends reflex HCV RNA testing following a positive HCV antibody result to promote uptake and reduce the time to viremia confirmation and treatment initiation. This can be achieved through laboratory-based reflex testing using stored specimens or clinic-based reflex testing with immediate specimen collection. Efforts should be made to minimize contamination risks when using stored specimens for reflex testing. The introduction of multi-disease testing platforms, both high-throughput lab-based and POC devices, offers opportunities for integration across programs, potentially expanding access and achieving cost savings. Countries with existing platforms for diseases such as HIV, TB, or SARS-CoV-2 can consider integrating HCV RNA testing. Pilot programs have demonstrated success with integrated lab-based and POC testing for HIV/TB and HIV/HCV. Operational considerations for POC assays include the need for strong decentralized systems, such as quality control, supply chain management, trained staff, and waste disposal. Infrastructure requirements depend on the device and assay, and should be reviewed prior to implementation. For example, near-POC technologies may require centrifugation, air conditioning, and dust-controlled environments. Unstable electricity may necessitate uninterruptible power supplies and voltage stabilizers. Research gaps include the need for rigorous implementation science studies to evaluate the use of POC platforms for HCV and HBV diagnosis and treatment decisions. Future studies should assess the effectiveness of diagnostic platforms across the continuum of care, including cost-effectiveness analyses. Evaluations should also examine the impact of integrated multi-disease testing platforms on access, uptake, turnaround times, and feasibility. In a feasibility study conducted in Yangon, Myanmar, a decentralized, community-based test-and-treat model for HCV care was implemented. POC testing included the Abbott SD Bioline HCV antibody rapid test and the Cepheid GeneXpert POC HCV viral load assay. General practitioners led the care, prescribing pangenotypic generic direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) to eligible participants. Testing and treatment services were provided on-site in a one-stop shop model. Of 633 participants recruited, 606 received HCV viral load testing, 488 initiated DAA treatment, 477 completed therapy, and 421 achieved SVR12. Staff reported that the GeneXpert device was simple to operate but sensitive to errors during specimen preparation, requiring precise pipetting skills.
